JSON: Name: sulfur_atom_trapping_lc_ms_pipeline Title: Sequential sulfur-atom trapping with IAM-TPP and isotope-dilution LC-MS/MS for simultaneous quantitative measurement of H2S, low-molecular-weight and protein persulfides and polysulfides in biological samples Short Hypothesis: Sequential alkylation with IAM-TPP followed by selective reduction with TCEP and isotope-dilution LC-MS/MS enables simultaneous, quantitative and chemically specific measurement of H2S, terminal sulfane sulfur from RSS−, internal sulfane sulfur from RS(S)n−, and GSS− in proteins, cell lysates and tissues with accuracy within ±15% and limits of detection ≤10 fmol per assay, outperforming conventional HPE-IAM and reduction-release methods. Related Work: Existing analytical approaches for reactive sulfur species quantify these analytes by either direct alkylation (e.g., HPE-IAM/TME-IAM), electrophilic trapping (monobromobimane), reduction-release followed by trapping (ethyl iodoacetate after reductive release), or phosphine-based sulfane atom incorporation. Direct alkylation methods provide site-specific protein labelling but suffer from limited sensitivity, incomplete distinction between H2S versus RSS−/RS(S)n− and potential loss of labile sulfur species. Electrophilic fluorogenic probes are sensitive but chemically non-selective and produce ambiguous species assignments in complex matrices. Reduction-release assays quantify total “liberable” H2S but conflate multiple sulfur reservoirs and are prone to artifacts from sample workup. Phosphine trapping can incorporate sulfane sulfur but is limited by phosphine oxidation and instability of phosphine–sulfur adducts. Across these methods there is a lack of: (1) simultaneous differentiation of H2S vs terminal vs internal sulfane sulfur, (2) isotope-dilution standardization for absolute quantification in tissues, (3) sub-fmol/low-fmol sensitivity with robustness to matrix effects, and (4) validated procedures that preserve volatile H2S during sample processing. Abstract: Problem: Current methods cannot simultaneously and quantitatively distinguish H2S, persulfide terminal sulfane atoms, polysulfide internal sulfane atoms, and glutathione persulfide (GSS−) in biological samples with high sensitivity and absolute accuracy. Approach: We present a structured pipeline that uses sequential sulfur-atom trapping: rapid alkylation with an iodoacetamide derivative bearing a triphenylphosphonium cation (IAM-TPP) to incorporate diagnostic sulfur-containing products, selective reduction with TCEP, and isotope-dilution liquid chromatography–tandem mass spectrometry (LC-MS/MS) with deuterated internal standards. Two complementary procedures are defined: Procedure A quantifies terminal sulfane sulfur and converts H2S into a readily detected TPP-tagged derivative; Procedure B quantifies internal sulfane sulfur in polysulfides and distinguishes low-molecular-weight versus protein-bound species. Contribution: The pipeline provides simultaneous measurement of H2S, RSS− terminal sulfur, RS(S)n− internal sulfur and GSS− across isolated proteins, cell lysates, mitochondria, and rodent tissues, with calibration for matrix effects and standard-addition workflows for absolute quantification. Expected outcome: A validated, reproducible assay suite delivering low-fmol sensitivity, linear quantitative readout across physiological concentrations, and the ability to distinguish changes in H2S from changes in persulfidation state in biological perturbations (e.g., ischemia or oxidative stress). Experiments: Overview: Validate analytical performance and test the hypothesis using in vitro standards, purified proteins, cultured cells, isolated mitochondria, ex vivo perfused heart, and in vivo rodent tissues under normoxia, ischemia and oxidative stress. Reagents and calibration: synthesize CAM-S-CAM-TPP, S(CAM-TPP)2, GS-CAM-TPP and GSS-CAM-TPP plus corresponding deuterated internal standards; prepare calibration curves in solvent and in pooled tissue extract matrix (0.001 μM–25 μM, include 0.001–0.1 μM points for low-fmol LOD determination); perform matrix-matched standard addition for tissues. Procedures: follow two trapping workflows: Procedure A (excess IAM-TPP alkylation → precipitation → reduction with 5 mM TCEP → excess IAM → LC-MS/MS) for terminal sulfane atoms and H2S; Procedure B (initial IAM alkylation → reduction with TCEP combined with excess IAM-TPP) for internal sulfane atoms. Sample sets and sample sizes: (1) in vitro chemical controls: GSH, GSSG, synthetic polysulfides at 6 concentrations, n=3 technical replicates each; (2) purified proteins: Trx1 (single Cys), recombinant Cofilin1, each treated with Na2S or Na2S2 at 5 concentrations, n=3 biological replicates; (3) HEK293 lysates: treated with Na2S/Na2S2 and DTNB, n=4 independent cultures; (4) isolated mouse heart mitochondria: treatments H2O2, Na2S, or combination, n=3 isolations; (5) Langendorff-perfused mouse hearts and in vivo LAD occlusion (heart) and MCAO (brain): normoxia vs ischemia vs ischemia+reperfusion, n=5 animals per group. Baselines and comparisons: compare IAM-TPP pipeline with (a) HPE-IAM-based trapping and LC-MS/MS; (b) monobromobimane fluorescence assay; (c) reductive-release ethyl iodoacetate-based total H2S assay. Experimental comparisons/ablations: (A1) Procedure A vs Procedure B on identical samples to quantify terminal vs internal sulfur assignment; (A2) IAM-TPP vs IAM (no TPP) to assess effect of TPP cation on sensitivity; (A3) varying TCEP incubation time (0.5, 3, 30 min) and concentration (0.1, 1, 5, 10 mM) to probe reduction-driven internal sulfur sequestration; (A4) ZnCl2 pre-treatment and CNBF thiol-block controls to assess contribution of free thiols vs persulfides; (A5) spike-recovery (standard addition) in tissues to validate absolute quantification. LC-MS/MS acquisition: MRM transitions for target compounds and deuterated standards; injection volume 2 μL on UPLC BEH C18 (1×50 mm, 1.7 μm), flow 0.2 mL/min, binary gradient as optimized; all samples run in randomized order with pooled QC every 8 injections. Evaluation metrics: limit of detection (LOD, S/N=3) and limit of quantification (LOQ, S/N=10) in fmol; calibration linearity (R2 ≥ 0.995); intra-assay and inter-assay precision (CV % ≤15); absolute recovery (% spike recovery within 85–115%); matrix effect (%) by comparing slope in matrix vs solvent; accuracy vs baselines by Passing–Bablok regression and Bland–Altman analysis; biological effect sizes for ischemia-induced H2S increase (report pmol/mg tissue and μM estimated tissue concentration). Statistical plan: minimum n=3 technical replicates per condition and n≥3–5 biological replicates; use paired t-test or ANOVA with Bonferroni correction for multiple comparisons; report 95% confidence intervals and effect sizes. Expected comparisons: IAM-TPP pipeline vs baselines for LOD, accuracy, and specificity; Procedure A vs B for differing assignments of terminal vs internal sulfane sulfur; TPP vs non-TPP for sensitivity enhancement. Risk Factors and Limitations: Chemical and procedural artifacts: volatile loss of H2S during sample handling and open systems may under-report H2S; TCEP-mediated nucleophilic attack can sequester internal sulfane sulfur causing underestimation of polysulfide internal sulfur if reduction conditions are not tightly controlled; alkylator-induced rearrangement (thioether formation) or disulfide isomerisation may alter diagnostic product distributions. Matrix and sensitivity limits: strong matrix effects in complex tissue extracts can suppress detection of deuterated GSS-CAM-TPP leading to higher LOD for GSS− than for CAM-S-CAM-TPP; heterogeneous tissue composition and variable protein binding challenge absolute quantification. Specificity constraints: IAM-TPP trapping relies on nucleophilicity differences; unusual sulfur chemistries or unexpected adducts in vivo could confound assignment between terminal and internal sulfur. Generalizability and throughput: protocol requires rapid snap-freezing, inert-gas handling, synthesized isotope-labelled standards and specialized LC-MS/MS instrument/time, limiting applicability in high-throughput or low-resource settings. Biological interpretation limits: bulk quantification does not provide cysteine-site resolution, subcellular compartmentalization, or real-time dynamics; low stoichiometry modifications may be below reliable quantification for regulatory conclusions. Statistical and sampling risks: biological variability across tissues and small n may limit power to detect small effect sizes; pre-analytical variability (time-to-freeze, handling) can bias results.
